KUBERNETES DEPRECATED API CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will this manifest survive your next Kubernetes upgrade?

Paste or load Kubernetes manifest YAML and get a deterministic report of every apiVersion + kind pair a past or future Kubernetes release has removed -- extensions/v1beta1 Ingress, batch/v1beta1 CronJob, policy/v1beta1 PodSecurityPolicy, and more.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device. No kubeconfig, no API server call.

1. Load your manifests

2. What this upgrade would break

Kind / nameStatusapiVersion usedReplacementRemoved in

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate before you upgrade?

Same table, zero dependencies, one file — run it against your manifest repo or your Helm/Kustomize render output:

node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml                              # list every known deprecated/removed API, exit 1 if any found
node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml --target-version 1.25        # exit 1 only if 1.25 would reject one of them
node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml --target-version 1.25 --strict --json

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It reads only the local file you name: no network call, ever.

What this checks — and what it cannot

The table below is sourced from Kubernetes' own Deprecated API Migration Guide, not guessed. It lists apiVersion+kind pairs across the four release waves that removed something (1.16, 1.22, 1.25, 1.26).

Already using Pluto from FairwindsOps? See how this checker differs — short version: same question, different install cost. Prefer to just read the guide and check by hand? See why that gets one apiVersion like extensions/v1beta1 Ingress wrong even when the rest of a check is correct. A manifest passing this check can still drop live traffic during the rollout itself for reasons that have nothing to do with a removed API — see Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check for readiness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets, and termination grace periods. Checking a chart rendered by Helm specifically? See Helm Values Schema Check for whether its values.yaml actually matches its own values.schema.json before you even render it. A manifest that survives the upgrade and drops no requests on rollout can still let one container starve or crowd out its whole node — see Kubernetes Resource Limits Check for missing memory/CPU/ephemeral-storage requests and limits.

Common questions

Does this catch every deprecated Kubernetes API?

No. It checks against a table of apiVersion+kind removals that Kubernetes' own Deprecated API Migration Guide documents with a fixed release number — currently the 1.16, 1.22, 1.25 and 1.26 removal waves. It deliberately does not guess at future or in-progress deprecations it cannot cite a release number for. Treat a clean report as one more gate passed, not a guarantee your manifests will survive every future upgrade.

Is my manifest uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses a pasted or locally loaded file entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads only a local file — no network call, ever.

Does this need a kubeconfig or talk to my cluster?

No. It reads only the YAML text you give it. It has no kubeconfig, makes no API server call, and needs no cluster access at all — that is what makes it safe to run against production manifests in CI.

Does it understand Helm charts or Kustomize overlays?

Not directly — it reads plain YAML documents, not Helm template expressions or Kustomize patches. Run helm template or kustomize build first and check the rendered output, the same manifest your cluster would actually receive.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not infrastructure, security, or compliance advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or Kubernetes' own release notes. It matches a fixed table of documented removals against the manifest you supplied — it cannot prove your manifests will apply cleanly on every future release, only report the matches it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for testing any upgrade against a non-production cluster first. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The manifest you load is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded, file_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Free and open source. If this saved you some digging, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

← Back to Kubernetes Deprecated API Check

This checker vs. checking the migration guide by hand

Kubernetes publishes its own Deprecated API Migration Guide, so a platform engineer can, in principle, read it and cross-check a manifest against it by eye. This page names no product or company: "reading the guide and checking by hand" is a manual habit anyone maintaining Kubernetes manifests already has, not a competing tool.

It genuinely works for a single manifest file checked right after reading the guide. It gets harder to trust the moment there is more than one file, more than one release wave to remember, or a kind that did not follow its apiVersion siblings' removal date -- which is exactly the case the table below covers.

CaseReading the guide and checking by handThis tool
A single manifest, checked right after reading the guideWorks fine -- the guide is short enough to hold in your head for one fileWorks the same way, instantly, with no re-reading required
extensions/v1beta1 Ingress among other extensions/v1beta1 kindsEasy to over-generalize: most extensions/v1beta1 kinds left in 1.16, but Ingress specifically stayed accepted until 1.22Looks up the exact apiVersion+kind pair, never the apiVersion alone, so Ingress is never misclassified against its siblings
A Helm chart or Kustomize overlay's rendered outputThe apiVersion a reviewer needs may only exist in the final render, not the source template -- has to be re-checked after every chart bump or values changeReads the rendered helm template / kustomize build output directly, document by document, every time
Comparing a found removedIn release against a target upgrade versionRequires parsing and comparing Kubernetes minor versions correctly by hand for every match -- string comparison alone gets "1.9" vs "1.22" wrongParses and compares versions numerically every time, reporting removed versus merely deprecated
Re-checking a manifest repo on every dependency bump or chart upgradeManual, and the first step skipped under deadline pressureCLI scans a whole render output in one pass; exits non-zero to block a CI gate

The gap that matters most: one kind that did not follow its own apiVersion's removal date

Four of the five kinds under extensions/v1beta1 -- DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, NetworkPolicy -- were removed in Kubernetes 1.16. Ingress under that same apiVersion stayed accepted for six more releases, until 1.22, per Kubernetes' own migration guide. A reviewer who has correctly learned "extensions/v1beta1 means the 1.16 wave" from checking the other four kinds will apply that same rule to an Ingress manifest and get the wrong answer in either direction -- clearing a manifest that is fine for six more releases as if it were already broken, or the reverse. This tool's table keys on the exact apiVersion+kind pair, so Ingress carries its own removedIn value independent of its siblings.

The gap that matters second: a rendered output nobody re-reads

A source Helm chart template or Kustomize base often does not name a fixed apiVersion at all -- it can come from a chart default, be overridden in values.yaml, or be patched by an overlay, and only becomes visible once you run helm template or kustomize build. Checking that rendered output by eye works the first time; it is the step most likely to be skipped after a routine chart version bump that "shouldn't have changed anything." This tool reads the same rendered output, document by document, with no dependency on remembering to re-run the check.

When to still read the guide yourself

This tool's table lists only removals Kubernetes has documented with a fixed release number -- it deliberately leaves out every in-progress or future-dated deprecation that has not shipped a removal release yet, and it has no cluster access, so it cannot tell you what your cluster is actually running today. Planning ahead for a still-beta deprecation, or understanding the reasoning behind a removal, is still a job for reading Kubernetes' own guide.

Common questions

Doesn't reading the migration guide once tell you everything this checks?

It tells you the facts this tool's table encodes -- Kubernetes publishes the guide and this tool's DEPRECATED_APIS table is sourced from it, not guessed. What reading it once does not do is re-check every apiVersion+kind pair in every manifest your Helm chart or Kustomize overlay renders, every time you edit one, against every release wave. That cross-referencing is the part that stops happening under time pressure, not the reading.

Why is it easy to over-generalize a removal wave to a kind it did not apply to?

The guide groups removals by release, and most extensions/v1beta1 kinds (DaemonSet, Deployment, ReplicaSet, NetworkPolicy) were removed in 1.16 -- but Ingress under the same apiVersion stayed accepted for six more releases, until 1.22. A hand-check that remembers "extensions/v1beta1 was the 1.16 wave" and applies that to every kind under it will wrongly clear an Ingress manifest that is actually fine until 1.22, or wrongly flag it as already broken. This tool looks up the exact apiVersion+kind pair, never the apiVersion alone.

Why does a rendered manifest repo make a hand-check harder than one file?

A Helm chart or Kustomize overlay can render dozens of documents across many templated files, and the apiVersion a reviewer needs to check is not always in the source template -- it can be set by a chart default, a values override, or a Kustomize patch, and only appears in the final helm template / kustomize build output. Reading the rendered output document by document, correctly, every time a chart version or values file changes, is the step a hand-check skips first under deadline pressure.

Can a target-version comparison be done by hand?

Yes, in principle: find each apiVersion+kind pair's removedIn release in the guide, then compare it against the target version you plan to upgrade to. In practice this means correctly parsing and comparing Kubernetes minor versions (is 1.22 before or after 1.9? -- string comparison gets this wrong) for every match, by hand, across every manifest. This tool does the version comparison the same way every time and reports removed versus merely deprecated-but-still-accepted.

When does reading the guide yourself still matter?

This tool's table only lists removals Kubernetes has documented with a fixed release number -- it deliberately excludes in-progress or future-dated deprecations that have not shipped a removal release yet. If you want to plan ahead for a deprecation that is still beta, or want the full context and rationale behind a removal, the guide itself is still the source to read.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or compliance advice. It matches a fixed table of documented removals against the manifest you supplied -- it cannot prove your manifests will apply cleanly on every future release, only report the matches it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything on the checker runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-pluto.html.text:
← Back to Kubernetes Deprecated API Check

This checker vs. Pluto

Pluto, maintained by FairwindsOps, is a widely used open-source Go tool for exactly this problem: finding deprecated or removed Kubernetes API versions. It ships as an installable binary (Homebrew, a GitHub release download, or a Docker image) with three scan modes -- local files, a rendered Helm chart or release, or, given cluster credentials, the API versions currently deployed in a live cluster -- backed by a version database FairwindsOps updates as each new Kubernetes release ships.

This checker answers the same underlying question with a much smaller footprint. It is a zero-dependency, zero-install browser page and a single Node file: paste or load manifest YAML, optionally name a target Kubernetes version, and get a report of every apiVersion + kind pair that release has removed or will remove. It has no cluster-scanning mode, no Helm-release introspection, and nothing to install: node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Scan a live cluster's currently deployed resources for deprecated API versions, with cluster credentials. Pluto -- that mode is built in.
Check a Helm release already installed in a cluster, or a chart's rendered output as part of a release pipeline. Pluto -- it has dedicated Helm-aware scanning.
Get the broadest, most current coverage of in-progress and future-dated deprecations, maintained release over release by a dedicated team. Pluto -- this checker deliberately lists only removals with a fixed release number already documented.
Check one manifest file or a small repo with nothing to install, no binary to pin a version of, and nothing uploaded anywhere. This checker -- open the page, paste or load the file, done.
Add a CI gate that is a single committed file with no external binary dependency to fetch, cache, or update. This checker -- cli.mjs is the whole dependency.
Get a pass/fail against a specific target Kubernetes version without installing anything first. This checker -- --target-version 1.25, right in the browser or the CLI.

These compose rather than compete. A team already running Pluto in its release pipeline for live-cluster or Helm-release scanning loses nothing by also keeping this narrower, install-free checker around for a quick one-off check on a manifest someone is about to hand-edit. And a team that does not want an external binary in its toolchain just for this one question can reach for this instead, with nothing to install at all. Neither replaces the other; they trade breadth and cluster-awareness for zero install cost in opposite directions.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Pluto?

They answer the same underlying question with different adoption costs. Pluto is a Go binary (install via Homebrew, a release download, or Docker) that can scan local files, a rendered Helm chart, or -- with cluster credentials -- a live cluster's currently deployed API versions, using its own maintained version database updated release by release. This tool is a zero-install browser page and a single dependency-free Node file: paste or load manifest YAML, optionally name a target Kubernetes version, get a report. If you want live-cluster scanning, Helm release introspection, or a tool already wired into a release pipeline, use Pluto. If you want a one-off check with nothing to install, or a CI gate that is a single committed file with no external dependency to pin and update, this is built for exactly that.

Does Pluto already cover what this checks?

For the specific removals this tool's table covers, yes -- both are checking the same underlying fact, sourced from the same place: Kubernetes' own Deprecated API Migration Guide. Pluto's database is broader and more actively maintained release over release, including in-progress deprecations this tool deliberately leaves out until a removal release is fixed. What differs is not the answer but what it costs to get one: Pluto needs installing and, for cluster or Helm-release scanning, credentials; this tool needs nothing but a browser tab or one Node file already sitting next to the manifest you want to check.

Why not just install Pluto instead of adding another tool?

Because they cost different amounts to adopt for a quick check. Pluto is a versioned binary with its own release cadence to track and, for live-cluster or Helm-release scanning, credentials to grant. This tool is one dependency-free JavaScript file: node cli.mjs check manifests.yaml, nothing to install, nothing to authenticate. If a team already runs Pluto in its release pipeline for the broader live-cluster and Helm-aware scanning it offers, this does not replace that -- it is a lighter, no-install option for a one-off check or a CI gate that should not depend on an external binary being present.

Is this page affiliated with Pluto or FairwindsOps?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Pluto or FairwindsOps, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not. What Pluto currently scans and how it is licensed are described on its own project page and repository -- check there for what it covers today.

Only point either tool at a manifest or cluster you own or are authorised to test. That rule is unchanged by which one you pick.

← Back to the checker

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or compliance advice. It matches a fixed table of documented removals against the manifest you supplied -- it cannot prove your manifests will apply cleanly on every future release, only report the matches it found. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

why-a-manifest-fails-a-kubernetes-upgrad.text:
← Back to Kubernetes Deprecated API Check

Why a manifest that applied yesterday fails after a Kubernetes upgrade

The mechanism

Kubernetes' API deprecation policy guarantees a minimum notice window before removing an API version — at least 12 months or 3 releases (whichever is longer) for a version that reached general availability, and at least 9 months or 3 releases for a beta. During that window the old and new versions of an object usually both work, converted automatically by the API server. At the end of it, the API server stops registering the old group/version for that kind entirely.

That is not a warning. kubectl apply, a rolling helm upgrade, or a controller's own reconcile loop against a manifest still written in the old apiVersion gets back no matches for kind "X" in version "Y" and the operation fails outright — nothing partially applies. A manifest that was correct on every prior cluster version becomes wrong the instant the cluster crosses the removal release, with no code change of its own.

Why this bites during an upgrade specifically

Most teams do not hand-write every manifest's apiVersion fresh each time — it gets copied from an older example, generated once by a scaffolding tool years ago, or left untouched inside a Helm chart or Kustomize base nobody has opened since it was written. It works, for years, right up until a managed control plane (EKS, GKE, AKS) is upgraded past the removal release, at which point the very first deploy after the upgrade is the one that fails — often mid-rollout, on a manifest nobody thought to look at because it had not changed.

The well-known removal waves so far: Kubernetes 1.16 removed the extensions/v1beta1 and apps/v1beta1/v1beta2 workload kinds; 1.22 removed a much larger batch spanning Ingress, RBAC, CRDs, admission webhooks, and more; 1.25 removed PodSecurityPolicy, CronJob's old batch version, PodDisruptionBudget's old policy version, and the first Horizontal Pod Autoscaler v2 beta; 1.26 removed the second HPA v2 beta. Each is documented with its exact release number in Kubernetes' own Deprecated API Migration Guide.

What this tool looks for, and why it stops where it does

Rather than trying to predict a future removal, this checks every apiVersion + kind pair in your manifest against a table built only from removals Kubernetes' own guide already documents with a fixed release number. Each entry names the release the old version stopped working and, where one exists, the exact replacement apiVersion to switch to.

It reads plain YAML text — apiVersion: and kind: as top-level keys, metadata.name for the report — and nothing else. It has no kubeconfig and makes no API server call, which is what makes it safe to run in CI against a manifest repository with no cluster credentials granted at all.

What this is not

This is not a Kubernetes admission controller, a cluster-connected scanner, or a guarantee your manifests will apply cleanly on every future release — the table only covers removals already documented with a release number, not every current beta or every proposed future change. It also does not evaluate Helm template expressions or Kustomize patches; run helm template or kustomize build first and check the rendered output, the same manifest your cluster would actually receive. And it says nothing about whether a rollout itself is safe once it applies — see Kubernetes Rollout Safety Check for readiness probes, disruption budgets, and termination grace periods, a separate failure class from a removed API entirely.

Common questions

Why does Kubernetes remove API versions instead of keeping them forever?

Every API version the server has to understand is code it has to keep correct and secure, and a beta API by definition was never meant to be permanent. Kubernetes' own deprecation policy commits to a minimum notice period — a GA API version is supported for at least 12 months or 3 releases (whichever is longer) after deprecation, and a beta is guaranteed at least 9 months or 3 releases — so there is always a documented window to migrate, but the version is not kept indefinitely.

What actually happens when you apply a manifest with a removed apiVersion?

The API server no longer registers that group/version for that kind at all, so kubectl apply, a Helm upgrade, or a controller's own reconcile loop gets back no matches for kind "X" in version "Y" and the operation fails outright — it is not a warning, and nothing partially applies.

Does upgrading kubectl or my CI tooling fix this?

No. The removal happens on the API server side, at the target cluster's Kubernetes version — the manifest's apiVersion field is what has to change, regardless of which kubectl or CI runner applies it.

No warranty. This is not infrastructure or compliance advice. See the disclaimer on the checker itself for the full text.

Everything here runs client-side; nothing is uploaded. Support is optional and never changes what the tool does.
